summary: The original sum of money borrowed or invested, before any interest.
The percentage charged or earned for the use of money, quoted per year unless stated otherwise.
detail: A nominal rate quoted per year can be applied monthly, daily or continuously — which is why the effective annual rate matters when comparing offers.

summary: The real yearly growth rate once compounding is taken into account: (1 + r/n)^n − 1.
detail: 6% nominal compounded monthly is about 6.168% effective — the number to compare between products.

summary: The equal periodic payment that pays off a loan with interest over a fixed term.
detail: M = P·i / (1 − (1+i)^−n), where i is the periodic rate and n the number of payments. Early payments are mostly interest; later ones mostly principal.

summary: A long-term loan secured against a property, usually repaid monthly over 15–30 years.
detail: Because the term is long, total interest often approaches or exceeds the amount borrowed. Overpaying early saves disproportionately more.

summary: Profit as a percentage of what you put in: (final − initial)/initial × 100.
detail: A 50% return over ten years is only about 4.1% a year compounded — annualising stops long projects looking better than they are.

summary: The steady yearly rate that would take a starting value to its ending value over the period: (final/initial)^(1/years) − 1.
The rate at which prices in general rise, eroding what money can buy.
detail: At 3% inflation, prices double in about 24 years (rule of 72: 72/3). Real return = nominal return − inflation.

summary: To find the years needed to double your money, divide 72 by the annual percentage rate.
detail: At 6% a year, 72/6 = 12 years to double. The exact answer is ln2/ln1.06 ≈ 11.9 years, so the rule is close and memorable.

summary: What a future sum is worth today once it is discounted at an interest rate.
detail: PV = FV/(1+r)^n. £1000 in five years is worth about £784 today at 5%.

summary: What an amount today becomes after compounding: FV = PV(1+r)^n.
The change between two values as a percentage of the original: (new − old)/|old| × 100.
detail: A 50% fall needs a 100% rise to recover — percentage changes are not symmetric.

summary: The sales level at which total revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero.
detail: Units = fixed costs / (price − variable cost per unit). Below it you lose money; above it each extra sale adds contribution margin.

summary: A compulsory charge on income, goods or services, usually a percentage of the price.
detail: VAT/GST is normally added to the quoted price, so the amount paid is price × (1 + rate/100). Income tax is usually banded, applying different rates to slices of income.
